A common failure mode is to mistake a segmented edge bar for clickable puzzle pieces. Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):

- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.

- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. - `current_frame.ascii` is a single newline-delimited string containing the latest board rendered with the letter-coded ARC color symbols.
- `current_frame.segmentation` parses the board into objects. It returns `{'nodes': [...], 'adjacency_list': [...]}`.
- Each node in `segmentation['nodes']` is one 4-connected same-color object with: `id` (index, ordered top-most-left-most), `color` (ARC color character), `hash` (a signature of the object's color and shape that ignores its position -- equal hashes mean the same object regardless of where it is, so use it to track an object across frames or to spot multiple identical objects in one frame), `pixels` (cell count), `boundary` (clockwise outer-perimeter corner points as `[row, col]`), and `children` (ids of objects fully enclosed by this one).
- `segmentation['adjacency_list']` is a list of `[i, j]` node-id pairs whose objects share an edge.
- `current_frame.step` is the current environment step count.
- `current_frame.level` is the current level number.
- `current_frame.shape` is a `(rows, cols)` tuple.
- The raw numeric grid is intentionally not exposed. Use `current_frame.segmentation` as your primary view of the board -- objects, colors, shapes, containment, adjacency, and cross-frame object hashes. Use `current_frame.ascii` only to read a small, specific region; do not scan the whole board with it.
- `history` is a chronological list of action/frame snapshots.
- `history` is a Python list of objects, not a dict.
- Each history entry exposes only `.action` and `.frame`; entries are not subscriptable like `entry['action']`.
- Each `history[i].frame` is the frame after `history[i].action`; each frame exposes only `.ascii`, `.step`, `.level`, `.shape`, and `.segmentation`.
- Important history semantics: when `history` is non-empty, `history[-1].frame` is the same latest/post-action board as `current_frame`. It is not the previous board. To inspect the state before the latest action, use `previous_frame` or `history[-2].frame` when available.
- `previous_frame` is the frame before the most recent real environment action, or `None` if no previous frame is available.

- `last_transition` is `transitions[-1]` or `None`. Its `.result` mirrors `last_action_result`; older transitions may have an empty `.result`. For before/after diffs, compare `last_transition.before_frame` to `last_transition.after_frame`; do not compare `current_frame` to `history[-1].frame`.

It remains available across later Python inspection calls that do not call `action(...)`, and is `{}` before any action result exists. Read transition metadata from fields/keys such as `last_action_result['board_changed']`, `last_action_result['done']`, `last_action_result['level_completed']`, `last_action_result['game_over']`, `last_action_result['run_complete']`, `last_action_result['reward']`, and `last_action_result['valid_actions']`.

Visual-game guidance:
- Treat each board as a scene with objects, blockers, targets, adjacency, containment, motion, and symmetry.
- Game entities are usually be rendered as connected multi-tile shapes such as 2×2, 2×3, 3×3, or longer patterned structures. Sometime they might also be 1x1 tokens.- Some games are logic or layout puzzles with no explicit player avatar or controllable sprite on the board. Do not assume a player exists; the relevant state may be an object, region, cursor, selector, or whole-board configuration.
- Background colors are often white or gray/black-ish large regions, but not always. Verify background hypotheses by area, stability, and object boundaries rather than assuming them.
- In many games, a long horizontal or vertical line near an edge is a timer or remaining-steps bar. It often shrinks or changes each step. If you identify such a bar, do not get distracted by it or treat it as core gameplay state unless there is concrete evidence that it interacts with the puzzle mechanics.
A common failure mode is to mistake a segmented edge bar for clickable puzzle pieces. If a repeated strip of small blocks sits flush against the top, bottom, left, or right border and actions only change that strip while the interior board stays the same, classify it as HUD/timer state, not as an object to click through segment by segment. DON'T DO THIS!
- Use coordinates only to target actions or describe local evidence. Do not frame the objective as reaching a specific absolute row or column.
- Re-ground on the newest frame after any score increase or abrupt scene change; the returned board may already be the next level.
- `WIN` means the whole game is solved. Mid-run level completion is more likely to appear as a score increase while play continues.
- Strategies may transfer loosely across levels, but layouts and mechanics can change. Re-check the new board before repeating a plan.
- For `MOUSE`, pass `row` and `col` integer arguments. `row` is vertical position, `col` is horizontal position.


Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.

Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.

- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.

The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.

A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.

- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.

- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.

Do not assume a player exists; the relevant state may be an object, region, cursor, selector, or whole-board configuration.
- Background colors are often white or gray/black-ish large regions, but not always. Verify background hypotheses by area, stability, and object boundaries rather than assuming them.
- In many games, a long horizontal or vertical line near an edge is a timer or remaining-steps bar. It often shrinks or changes each step. If you identify such a bar, do not get distracted by it or treat it as core gameplay state unless there is concrete evidence that it interacts with the puzzle mechanics.
A common failure mode is to mistake a segmented edge bar for clickable puzzle pieces. If a repeated strip of small blocks sits flush against the top, bottom, left, or right border and actions only change that strip while the interior board stays the same, classify it as HUD/timer state, not as an object to click through segment by segment. Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.

Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.

If you identify such a bar, do not get distracted by it or treat it as core gameplay state unless there is concrete evidence that it interacts with the puzzle mechanics.
A common failure mode is to mistake a segmented edge bar for clickable puzzle pieces. If a repeated strip of small blocks sits flush against the top, bottom, left, or right border and actions only change that strip while the interior board stays the same, classify it as HUD/timer state, not as an object to click through segment by segment. DON'T DO THIS!
- Use coordinates only to target actions or describe local evidence. Do not frame the objective as reaching a specific absolute row or column.
- Re-ground on the newest frame after any score increase or abrupt scene change; the returned board may already be the next level.
- `WIN` means the whole game is solved. Mid-run level completion is more likely to appear as a score increase while play continues.
- Strategies may transfer loosely across levels, but layouts and mechanics can change. Re-check the new board before repeating a plan.
- For `MOUSE`, pass `row` and `col` integer arguments. `row` is vertical position, `col` is horizontal position.


Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.

  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape.   C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it.   B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.

  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape.   D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.

  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.

Do not assume a player exists; the relevant state may be an object, region, cursor, selector, or whole-board configuration.
- Background colors are often white or gray/black-ish large regions, but not always. Verify background hypotheses by area, stability, and object boundaries rather than assuming them.
- In many games, a long horizontal or vertical line near an edge is a timer or remaining-steps bar. It often shrinks or changes each step. If you identify such a bar, do not get distracted by it or treat it as core gameplay state unless there is concrete evidence that it interacts with the puzzle mechanics.
A common failure mode is to mistake a segmented edge bar for clickable puzzle pieces. If a repeated strip of small blocks sits flush against the top, bottom, left, or right border and actions only change that strip while the interior board stays the same, classify it as HUD/timer state, not as an object to click through segment by segment. Field guide (patterns seen across many ARC-AGI-3 games; treat as hypotheses to confirm, never as facts):
- These are small human-designed puzzle games: always solvable, level 1 is a tutorial, and each later level usually adds exactly one new mechanic on top of the previous ones. Reuse what you learned, but re-check it on the new board.
- First ask "what is this level asking me to do", only then "what does each action do". A common goal shape: make the region you CAN change look like the region you CANNOT change (answer area vs. pattern/template). Cells no action ever changes are the template.
- Common families and how to play them:
  A) Copy the pattern: a template and an answer area side by side. Find out what the "brush" is (big brush / small brush / color change / pick-a-part-and-place); later paint covers earlier paint. A small patterned 3x3 block is often a blueprint for how its own neighbourhood must be filled.
  B) Navigate and unlock: pressing arrow keys moves one ~5x5 block as a whole -- that block is you. A small panel in a corner shows your current shape/color; a room's display shows the target shape. Step on map gadgets (rotators / shape changers / color changers) to become the target shape AND color, then walk into that room. Walking costs energy (an energy bar); running out teleports you back to the start, so do not wander: learn each key's effect, plan the whole route, then walk it, avoiding cells that would change your shape/color after you have it.
  C) Push the box: a movable block and a slot. You can push, not pull; do not push it into a corner.
  D) Lights-out: clicking one cell flips a region. Learn the flip pattern first, then decide the set of cells to click before clicking.
  E) Dictionary translation: paired examples plus a fill-in area. Induce the mapping from the examples, cycle through candidates with the cycle key, and the level completes by itself when everything matches.
  F) Draw a spell: a small canvas, a hint pattern, a character and an exit. Drawing the right pattern casts a skill; you win by walking the character into the exit, not by drawing.
  G) Chain reaction / collect: click a key position to trigger a big cascade, or gather scattered pieces into slots; prefer centres, gaps and symmetry points.
  H) Extend-and-retract pipes: coloured 3-wide segments joined end to end; a box per colour has a shorten and a lengthen cell (3 cells per press); a small box rotates a segment and everything after it. The goal is to park the tip (the small dot near the end) exactly on a diamond marker. Growth is blocked by walls (a blocked press is wasted), later segments ride along when an earlier one changes, segments of the same colour share one box, and all targets must be satisfied at the same time.
  I) Tanks and boats: black = water, thin light lines = pipes, small square buttons come in pairs flanking a pipe and pour water between the two tanks at its ends (total water is conserved); a boat floats on the water. A plug inside a pipe is a gate: when the water on both sides is level with it, clicking it moves the boat to the neighbouring tank (the move plays as an animation over the next few frames). Win by bringing each boat to the row of its same-coloured gate.
- Counters: a row or column near an edge that changes every step regardless of what you do is a step counter, not a mechanic; ignore it when comparing frames.
- If something does not change on the very next frame, do not conclude it did nothing: some effects (gates, animations, level transitions) show up a step or two later.
- Some effects happen only under a precondition (right shape, water level, order of clicks). If an action does nothing, ask what precondition is missing instead of repeating it.
